name: DOM downsampling for LLM web agents. Not one artifact but a fast-moving cluster of techniques for reducing a page's DOM to something a model can afford to read. Named systems: D2Snap (Beyond Pixels: Exploring DOM Downsampling for LLM-Based Web Agents, arXiv:2508.04412), Prune4Web (DOM Tree Pruning Programming for Web Agent, arXiv:2511.21398), FocusAgent (Simple Yet Effective Ways of Trimming the Large Context of Web Agents, arXiv:2510.03204), LineRetriever (Planning-Aware Observation Reduction for Web Agents, arXiv:2507.00210), PageDigest, Region4Web (Rethinking Observation Space Granularity for Web Agents, arXiv:2605.07134), and AgentOccam-style attribute and node pruning. Adjacent older work that these effectively rediscover: Chromium's DOM Distiller, Mozilla Readability, and Boilerpipe -- all covered separately in this research set, and all doing structure-based content selection for humans rather than for agents.
kind: Research results plus reference implementations. Not a standard, not a browser feature, not a service. The category is a set of competing algorithms for the same problem, with no shared benchmark protocol and no agreed evaluation metric beyond downstream task success.
maturity: Research-prototype throughout, and very new -- the substantive papers date from 2025 and 2026, with several appearing within months of each other and not citing one another. Nothing here is production-hardened or widely deployed; the production practice it competes with is the accessibility tree (item 28), which most agent harnesses adopted precisely because it is a downsampling that the browser already performs. The rapid proliferation of mutually-unaware methods is itself the field's diagnostic signal: there is no accepted answer and no accepted way to compare answers.
license: Mixed and mostly unstated in the papers. Reference implementations released alongside arXiv preprints are typically MIT or Apache-2.0 when released at all, and several of these papers have no public code. Nothing appears to be licence-blocked for use here, but nothing is confirmed either; and since the recommendation below is to adopt mechanisms rather than code, licence is largely moot. [uncertain] on every specific implementation's licence.
keeps_and_discards: Each method draws the keep/discard line differently and the differences map exactly onto how much structural judgement each one imports. D2SNAP downsamples by CONSOLIDATING nodes, explicitly framed by its authors as image compression applied to HTML, with the stated preservation target being 'actionability and actionability-discriminating features' -- so it keeps whatever distinguishes one interactive element from another and merges or drops the rest, and it is the most nearly structure-agnostic of the group because its criterion is interactivity rather than semantics. PRUNE4WEB keeps whatever a generated scoring script scores highly: an LLM writes an executable Python scoring function against the DOM and the DOM is filtered programmatically, so the model never reads the raw DOM at all and what survives is whatever the task-specific script selected. FOCUSAGENT and LINERETRIEVER keep task-relevant content and discard the rest, using retrieval or planning-awareness to decide relevance. PAGEDIGEST and REGION4WEB keep a re-granulated summary. What is discarded across all of them, and this is the common and under-reported cost: attribute noise (class strings, framework-generated ids, data-* attributes), non-interactive wrapper elements, repeated sibling structure, and -- in the relevance-based methods -- anything the relevance model did not associate with the current task, which necessarily includes anything a future task would need. The one thing every method preserves is the ability to ACT, because a downsampled observation that loses the target element makes the task unsolvable and shows up immediately in the score; the thing every method quietly loses is READING fidelity, because content that is not needed to click something is dropped and no metric in this literature measures it.
structure_preserved: Partially and inconsistently. D2Snap consolidates nodes, so hierarchy survives in compressed form -- parent-child relations are preserved for surviving nodes, and the collapsing of chains is analogous to the path compression a patricia trie does, which is why it is the closest fit to this project's shape. Prune4Web filters nodes and preserves the tree over what remains. Line-oriented methods (LineRetriever) operate over a serialised representation and preserve reading order but not necessarily containment. Region-granularity methods re-segment the page into blocks, which is the largest structural intervention and the least recoverable. Across all of them, the critical loss for this project is ADDRESSABILITY: a downsampled node's relationship to the original DOM address is preserved only if the method carries an identifier through, and most of these papers carry an agent-facing element id rather than a durable address, so the downsampled artifact cannot be re-joined to a stored capture. Shadow boundaries are not mentioned in any of these papers; they all operate on a flattened HTML serialisation and none of them discusses composed-tree or shadow-root handling, which is a straightforward gap given how much modern application UI lives in shadow roots.
interactive_elements: Interactivity is the field's organising principle, which is a striking and useful convergence. D2Snap's stated preservation criterion is actionability and actionability-discriminating features -- it keeps what you can act on and what tells two actionable things apart, which is very nearly a restatement of this project's 'tag plus interactivity'. Prune4Web's evaluation metric is low-level sub-task GROUNDING accuracy, i.e. did the pruned DOM still contain and identify the element the action needed. Every method assigns stable per-element identifiers to whatever survives so the agent can reference a target. The convergence is evidence that interactivity is a sufficient and largely structure-agnostic selection criterion for actionable use -- but note what it implies about the other half: none of these methods is evaluated on whether the CONTENT a reader needs survived, only on whether the CONTROL an actor needs survived. A fold that must serve reading as well as acting cannot inherit their evaluation and should not inherit their thresholds.
interactive_state_fidelity: Barely addressed, and it is the field's most consequential omission. These methods operate on serialised HTML, so they inherit the attribute/property split described in item 26: the disabled attribute survives downsampling, a checkbox's actual checkedness does not exist in the input at all. D2Snap's actionability-discriminating criterion in principle should keep state-bearing attributes, since two otherwise-identical buttons distinguished only by disabled are actionability-discriminating, but no paper reports state preservation as a measured property. Since a large class of agent failures is acting on a control whose state the agent misread, and since the accessibility tree's whole advantage is that it resolves computed state, a downsampler that operates on markup starts from a strictly poorer input than the AXTree it is competing with, and none of these papers acknowledges it. Practical consequence for the project: whatever downsampling is adopted must run over a representation that already carries read-in IDL state, or the state is gone before the downsampler sees it.
layout_awareness: Mostly none, and that is the category's main appeal here -- these are text-in, text-out algorithms over HTML. D2Snap is explicitly positioned against the pixel/screenshot alternative, and its central empirical claim is that a downsampled DOM does at least as well as a grounded GUI baseline without any geometry. Region-granularity methods are the exception to watch: re-segmenting a page into regions can be done structurally (by container nesting) or visually (by rendered position), and the visual variant would import geometry. For the project, the layout-free members of this family sit cleanly inside the fold and the visually-segmented ones do not.
javascript_required: The DOM being downsampled has to exist, so in practice these run against a live rendered page in a browser harness. The downsampling itself is a pure function of the serialised DOM and requires no scripts to run, which means it can equally be applied offline to a stored capture -- an important property that these papers do not exploit and that the project should: downsampling a stored getHTML artifact is reproducible, re-runnable at different budgets, and testable, whereas downsampling live is none of those.
evaluation_method: Downstream task success on web-agent benchmarks, with the downsampler swapped in and out. This is the right general approach and it is executed with widely varying rigour. D2Snap evaluates on a dataset sampled from Online-Mind2Web with GPT-4o and reports success rate with a confidence interval -- reporting the interval is unusually honest and, as it turns out, decisive. Prune4Web reports low-level sub-task grounding accuracy, which is a narrower and easier metric than end-to-end task success and is not directly comparable to the others. FocusAgent and PageDigest evaluate on WebArena and WorkArena with success rate and token count. Nobody uses the same protocol as anybody else, nobody re-implements a competitor as a baseline, and the comparisons in each paper are against a raw-DOM or screenshot control rather than against the other methods. The structural problem is that success rate on a benchmark task is a very coarse proxy for whether a downsampler preserved a page: an agent can succeed while the downsampler discarded 90% of the content, because the task only needed one button. There is no fidelity metric in this literature at all -- no measurement of what fraction of a page's content, affordances or state survives -- which means the field measures usefulness for one narrow purpose and calls it compression quality.
corpus_size_and_origins: Small and heterogeneous. D2Snap uses a sample from Online-Mind2Web, which draws from real live websites and is therefore the most origin-diverse evaluation in the group, but the paper does not state the sample size in its abstract and the reported confidence interval implies it is small. WebArena-based evaluations (FocusAgent, PageDigest) run on FIVE self-hosted simulated sites, which is the reach problem described in item 28 and is severe for a compression claim specifically: benchmark clones lack the advertising, consent overlays, third-party embeds, tracking pixels and A/B-test scaffolding that make real DOMs enormous, so a downsampler tuned on them is tuned on the easy case. Prune4Web's corpus is not clear from the abstract. Aggregate: nothing here approaches 136 pages from 109 origins, and the one live-web evaluation (D2Snap on Online-Mind2Web) is the one whose result turns out to be statistically inconclusive. [uncertain] on exact sample sizes for D2Snap and Prune4Web.
reported_precision_recall: Success rates and token counts, reported here with their denominators and their uncertainty, because the uncertainty is the most important part. D2SNAP, on a sample from Online-Mind2Web with GPT-4o: 42% of RAW DOM snapshots exceeded the model's 128,000-token context window, while ALL D2Snap-downsampled snapshots fit, with a mean context utilisation of 16.5%; success rate 73% for D2Snap versus 67% for the grounded-GUI (screenshot) baseline, a gain of 5.8 percentage points -- BUT with a 95% confidence interval of -13.6 to +26.0 percentage points, which straddles zero comfortably and means the comparison is NOT statistically distinguishable from no difference. That interval must be quoted whenever the 73%-versus-67% figure is, because the headline reads as a win and the interval says the study cannot tell. The same paper reports grounding text alone attaining 62% and concludes that image input appears to add little to snapshot utility -- consistent with the independent screenshot null result in item 28, and the agreement between two unrelated studies is the strongest evidence in this area that screenshots are not earning their token cost. PRUNE4WEB: low-level sub-task grounding accuracy from 46.80% to 88.28% -- a very large improvement, but on a grounding sub-metric rather than end-to-end success, and reported by the method's own authors against their own baseline. PAGEDIGEST: observation length reduced 43% on average, from 6,437 to 3,671 tokens, with task success improved by 2.3 percentage points across four backbone models on WebArena -- the most solid result in the group because it holds across four models. GENERAL SCALE FIGURE, widely repeated: raw DOM commonly 10,000 to 100,000 tokens. The honest summary: the token reductions are real and large; the accuracy claims range from well-supported-and-modest (PageDigest, +2.3pp across four models) to statistically inconclusive (D2Snap) to narrow-metric and author-run (Prune4Web).
independent_oracle: The benchmark's own task checker is a real independent oracle for TASK SUCCESS -- it verifies final environment state programmatically without sharing assumptions with the downsampler. It is not an oracle for COMPRESSION FIDELITY, and none exists in this literature. That is the central methodological gap: the field has a good oracle for the wrong question. The oracle-free fidelity metrics this project cares about (item 9) -- recall against the source, compression ratio reported alongside it, and round-trip fixed points -- are precisely what would fill the gap, and applying them to these downsamplers would be a straightforward contribution. A cheap partial oracle available immediately: run the downsampler, then check that every element the task's ground-truth action targets survived, aggregated over all tasks -- that measures affordance recall directly rather than inferring it from success, and no paper reports it.
evidence_independence: Author-run throughout, with no cross-evaluation. Every number in this item was produced by the authors of the method it describes, using a baseline they configured, on a corpus they chose, with no independent replication and no head-to-head comparison between methods. That is normal for a young field and it means the numbers cannot be ranked against each other -- D2Snap's 73% and PageDigest's +2.3pp and Prune4Web's 88.28% are measurements of different things on different corpora with different models and are not comparable in any direction. The one methodological practice that raises confidence is reporting confidence intervals (D2Snap) and reporting across multiple backbone models (PageDigest, four models); the practice that lowers it is reporting a single narrow sub-metric against a single self-configured baseline. Cross-study AGREEMENT on the screenshot null result -- D2Snap's 'image input appears to add little' and the independent Fisher's-exact null in item 28 -- is the one place where two independent groups converge, and it is therefore the most trustworthy claim in the whole area.
page_archetype_coverage: Unreported and mechanically important. Downsampling gain is a function of DOM redundancy, which varies enormously by archetype: a listing or collection page with hundreds of near-identical sibling subtrees is where consolidation-based methods (D2Snap) should win by an order of magnitude, because that is exactly the structure they compress; a documentation or article page has little redundant structure and a downsampler mostly strips attributes; an application shell is dominated by framework noise, where attribute pruning dominates; a product page mixes a redundant gallery with dense unique content. Since the WebArena environments are a shopping site, a shopping admin, a forum, a code host and a map, the benchmark is actually reasonably spread over listing-heavy archetypes and poorly spread over article and documentation archetypes -- which biases the measured gains upward relative to a reading-oriented corpus. No paper breaks results down this way and any single compression ratio conceals the spread.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Entirely unexamined; every evaluation is English. Two mechanical hazards follow. First, token-count-based claims do not transfer across scripts: CJK text costs substantially more tokens per character under common BPE tokenisers, so a 43% reduction measured on English pages is not a 43% reduction in the practical budget on a Japanese page, and a downsampler tuned to a token budget will behave differently. Second, any method that scores or ranks content by relevance depends on the embedder's or model's quality in the page's language, so relevance-based pruning (FocusAgent, LineRetriever, Prune4Web's scoring scripts) degrades in low-resource languages in a way that structural consolidation (D2Snap) does not. That is a real argument for preferring structural consolidation over relevance ranking on script-invariance grounds alone, independent of the structure_agnosticism constraint. [uncertain] -- inference from mechanism; no measurement exists.
leaks_outward: Downsampling is an in-process transformation and leaks nothing to the page. Its privacy significance is entirely on the other side: it determines how much page content is sent to the model, so a downsampler is a data-minimisation mechanism whether or not it is designed as one. A method that reduces a page from 100,000 to 16,000 tokens reduces by the same proportion the personal data disclosed to a hosted model. This is never framed this way in the papers and it is one of the clearer arguments for aggressive default budgets in any pipeline that sends observations off-machine.
mechanism_detectability: Zero -- downsampling happens after the page is read and the page cannot observe it. The detectability question belongs entirely to the upstream capture, and this is worth stating because it means the choice of downsampler is unconstrained by detectability considerations, unlike the choice of capture mechanism (item 28). One second-order note: methods that require a live browser round trip per pruning decision, or that inject instrumentation to score elements, would inherit the capture layer's detectability; the methods surveyed here operate on an already-captured serialisation and do not.
countermeasures: FocusAgent makes the security argument explicitly and it is the most interesting claim in this item: trimming reduces the attack surface by removing extraneous content where adversarial injections could hide, thereby lowering vulnerability to prompt injection. That is a genuine and under-appreciated dual benefit -- compression as a safety mechanism, because injected content in a region the downsampler discards never reaches the model. It is also a trap, and the trap should be stated: the reduction in exposure is only as reliable as the downsampler's coverage, an attacker who knows the downsampling rule can place the injection in content the downsampler KEEPS (interactive elements, task-relevant text, high-scoring regions), and a relevance-based downsampler is specifically vulnerable because attacker-authored text can be written to score highly on task relevance. So downsampling raises the cost of a naive injection and lowers the cost of a targeted one, and its net effect against an adaptive adversary is unmeasured. No paper evaluates a downsampler against an adaptive attacker.
measured_fidelity_cost: Measured only as downstream task success, never as content fidelity, and this is the field's defining gap. Against a raw-DOM control, PageDigest's 43% reduction cost -2.3 percentage points of success (i.e. it gained), D2Snap's reduction to 16.5% mean context utilisation cost an amount indistinguishable from zero given its confidence interval, and Prune4Web's pruning gained 41.5 points of grounding accuracy over its baseline. Read together, these say that compressing an agent observation by 40-85% has no measurable cost to acting and may help. What is NOT measured anywhere: how much of the page's readable content survives, how many affordances survive, whether state survives, and whether a second, different task could still be performed from the downsampled observation. The project's own measured position -- a projection drawing 80.9% of a page's affordances against a capture holding 99.7% -- is exactly the measurement this literature lacks, and it means the project is already ahead of the published state of the art on the metric that matters for reading rather than acting.
gate_state_at_capture: Not represented, and there is a specific hazard worth naming. A consent overlay, paywall interstitial or login wall is typically a large, highly interactive, visually and structurally prominent region -- exactly the kind of content that an actionability-preserving downsampler will KEEP and that a relevance-based downsampler may DISCARD as task-irrelevant. So the same gated page produces radically different downsampled observations depending on the method, and in the relevance-based case the model may be handed a page with the paywall silently removed and the underlying content missing, which is an incoherent observation with no error. Gate state must be detected and recorded before downsampling, not inferred after.
determinism: Splits the field cleanly and is the single most important axis for this project. STRUCTURAL methods -- D2Snap's node consolidation, attribute pruning, sibling collapsing -- are pure deterministic functions of the DOM: same input, same output, always, and re-runnable offline. LLM-DEPENDENT methods are not. Prune4Web has an LLM generate an executable Python scoring script per task, which means the pruning rule itself is sampled from a model and differs between runs; the pruning is then deterministic given the script, but the script is not, so the pipeline as a whole is non-deterministic and its output is not reproducible without storing the generated script as an artifact. Retrieval-based methods (FocusAgent, LineRetriever) are deterministic given a fixed embedder and fixed thresholds, and drift when either changes. For a project that requires reproducibility, this ordering is decisive: structural consolidation is adoptable, generated-script pruning is not adoptable without pinning and storing the generated rule, and even then it is reproducible only in replay.
determinism_across_versions: Structural downsamplers are stable across versions of themselves and vary only with the HTML parser that produced the DOM -- the same narrow drift surface as any DOM-based method, and the smallest in this research set. LLM-based downsamplers drift with every model change, and since hosted models change silently behind stable API names, a pruning rule generated in one month is not reproducible in the next; this is the same irreproducibility that afflicts all agent research (item 27) but it is worse here because the model is inside the DATA PATH rather than only inside the decision loop, so it affects the stored artifact and not just the trajectory. Embedding-based relevance methods drift with embedder version. Recommendation: any downsampling in a reproducible pipeline should be a pinned, versioned, pure function, with the version recorded in the artifact.
reproducibility: Poor for the field, achievable for the mechanism. Field-level: no shared protocol, no head-to-head comparisons, several papers without public code, live-web evaluation corpora that cannot be refrozen, and hosted models that no longer exist in the form measured. Mechanism-level: a structural downsampler applied to a stored getHTML capture is perfectly reproducible and can be re-run at any budget, which is a strong argument for separating CAPTURE (once, stored, lossless) from DOWNSAMPLING (many times, cheap, versioned, pure). The papers all conflate the two by downsampling live, which forecloses re-running at a different budget and makes their own results unre-derivable.
failure_modes: (1) DROPPING THE NEEDED ELEMENT -- the canonical failure, and the one every paper optimises against; the agent then cannot complete the task and, worse, has no way to know why. (2) SILENT CONTENT LOSS -- content dropped for reading purposes, invisible because no metric measures it. (3) RELEVANCE MODEL FAILURE -- for retrieval- and score-based methods, an off-target relevance judgement discards the right content confidently; this is a classifier failure and it is not detectable from the output. (4) GENERATED-RULE FAILURE -- Prune4Web's scoring script can be wrong or can fail to execute, and the failure mode of a generated program is unbounded. (5) STRUCTURE DESTRUCTION -- over-aggressive consolidation merges nodes whose distinction mattered, and since consolidation is lossy there is no recovery. (6) ADDRESS LOSS -- the downsampled artifact cannot be joined back to the source unless identifiers are carried, which most methods do only for the agent's current session. (7) ADAPTIVE ADVERSARY -- an injection placed in content the downsampler preserves passes through with the noise stripped away around it, arguably MORE salient than before. (8) ARCHETYPE MISMATCH -- a downsampler tuned on listing-heavy benchmark sites under-performs on prose-heavy pages, where there is little redundancy to remove and the pruning starts cutting content.
failure_visibility: Silent in every case, which is the field's worst property and the easiest to fix. A downsampled observation looks like a page. Nothing marks what was consolidated, what was dropped, how much was dropped, or why. An agent reading a downsampled DOM cannot tell whether the button it needs is absent because it does not exist or because it was pruned, and cannot ask for more. No paper in this group emits elision markers or a residual-content indicator. The fix is cheap and is the same one item 27's ACI evidence supports: every consolidation and every drop should leave a marker stating what class of thing was removed and how many, so that absence is distinguishable from emptiness and the model can request expansion. This is also what makes downsampling compatible with a pay-for-the-child-list design rather than opposed to it -- a marker is an offer to expand.
scale_limits: The problem being solved is itself a scale limit: raw DOM commonly runs 10,000-100,000 tokens and D2Snap's measurement that 42% of raw snapshots exceeded a 128,000-token context window quantifies how often the naive approach simply fails. Post-downsampling, D2Snap reports a mean context utilisation of 16.5%, so the technique moves the binding constraint from 'does it fit' to 'is it useful'. The remaining scale limit is the trajectory: observations accumulate across steps, so even a 16.5% per-step observation exhausts context in a handful of steps, which means downsampling alone does not solve the multi-step budget and must be combined with transcript management. Compute cost: structural methods are linear in DOM size and negligible; LLM-based methods add a model call per page, which can cost more than the tokens saved; embedding-based methods add an embedding pass per candidate region.
delta_cost_model: None of these methods has one -- every one recomputes the downsampled observation from the full DOM at every step, which is O(page) per step by construction and is the reason the field's cost story is about fitting rather than about incrementality. The transferable question is whether downsampling COULD be incremental, and the answer differs by method in a way worth recording. Structural consolidation is locally computable: whether a node collapses depends on its own subtree, so a mutation to a subtree requires recomputing only that subtree's consolidation, and the cost is O(affected subtree). What falls OUTSIDE that bound: (1) consolidation decisions that depend on SIBLING SIMILARITY -- collapsing repeated list items requires comparing siblings, so one changed sibling can change the consolidation of its whole sibling group, amplifying a one-node delta to O(siblings); (2) any GLOBAL BUDGET, since a fixed token budget means adding content anywhere forces trimming somewhere else, which is a global constraint that no local update can satisfy -- this is the fundamental reason budgeted output is not O(delta) and it must be named; (3) RELEVANCE-BASED methods entirely, since relevance is computed against the whole page and a task, so any change can in principle change every score; (4) LLM-GENERATED pruning rules, which are regenerated per task and are O(page) per generation with no incremental form; (5) the initial full downsample; (6) everything the underlying capture cannot see (item 24's list), which no downsampler can recover. The honest conclusion is that structural, budget-free downsampling is compatible with an O(delta) design at O(affected subtree plus sibling group) cost, and that any globally-budgeted or relevance-ranked downsampling is not.
reanchoring_stability: Weak and mostly unaddressed. These methods assign session-scoped element identifiers for the agent to reference and do not carry durable addresses, so a downsampled observation from one load cannot be aligned with one from the next. Consolidation makes this worse: when several nodes merge into one, the merged node's identity is a function of the merge, so a DOM change that alters what merges alters identities of things that did not themselves change -- an amplification of exactly the kind item 23 warns about. The mitigation, if downsampling is adopted here, is to make every surviving node carry the ORIGINAL address (or the set of addresses it consolidates), so the projection is a view over the trie rather than a separate artifact. That costs a few tokens per node and preserves the join, and no published method does it.
adversarial_exposure: Two-sided, and the balance is unmeasured. On the protective side, FocusAgent's explicit claim that trimming reduces the injection attack surface is real for non-adaptive attacks: content that never reaches the model cannot instruct it, and a method that discards 85% of a page discards most randomly-placed injections along with it. On the exposed side, three problems. First, adaptive placement -- an attacker who knows or guesses the downsampling rule places the payload where it survives, and interactive elements and task-relevant text are both preserved by design and easy to author. Second, relevance-based methods are actively invertible: the payload can be written to maximise relevance to plausible tasks, so the downsampler becomes a targeting aid. Third, and specific to this project's constraint, none of these methods reads layout, so none can filter rendering-based concealment -- a display:none block containing an injection is, to a structural downsampler, ordinary content, and if it happens to contain interactive elements or high-scoring text it will be preserved preferentially. That means downsampling does not raise the layout-blind ceiling described in item 28; it only reduces the volume of what passes through it. What downsampling CAN do without geometry, and should, is act as the enforcement point for the layout-free concealment checks: since every node passes through the downsampler anyway, it is the natural place to apply Unicode-level normalisation and screening, attribute-declared hiding checks (hidden, aria-hidden, inert, tabindex=-1) and inline-style-attribute string inspection, and to mark rather than silently drop anything that trips them -- marking rather than dropping matters, because silently removing suspicious content destroys the evidence that an injection was attempted.
provenance_carrying: None natively; this is a uniform gap. Downsampled output is text with agent-facing ids and no url, no address, no capture time, no shadow depth and no gate state. Since the downsampler is the last stage before the model sees anything, it is the correct and only place to attach provenance in a form the model actually reads, and the fact that no method does so is the clearest single deficiency in the group. For this project the fix is nearly free because the trie key is already the provenance: a downsampler operating over trie nodes rather than over a flat serialisation can emit the address alongside each surviving node, and consolidation can emit the address set it merged. Provenance the model cannot see cannot affect how the model treats content, so this must be inline, not side-channel.
roundtrip_safety: Lossy by design, so serialise-parse-serialise is not a fixed point and cannot be -- consolidation discards information deliberately. That does not make round-trip testing useless; it makes it a different test. The useful invariant is IDEMPOTENCE: downsampling an already-downsampled observation should be a no-op, and if it is not, the method's stopping condition is ill-defined. A second useful invariant is MONOTONICITY IN BUDGET: the output at budget 2B should be a superset of the output at budget B, which is what makes progressive expansion coherent and which no paper checks. Both are free, oracle-free tests. Escaping is a real hazard at this stage specifically: downsamplers emit page content into a structured text format (indented trees, pseudo-markdown, tagged lines) and page content containing that format's delimiters will corrupt the structure -- none of these papers discusses escaping, and it is the same class of problem as item 15's markdown injection vector.
token_budget_and_ordering: This is the item's main deliverable and the numbers are usable. (1) THE COMPRESSION IS FREE OR BETTER at the ratios measured: 43% reduction with +2.3pp success across four models (PageDigest); reduction to 16.5% mean context utilisation with a success difference indistinguishable from zero (D2Snap). Two independent studies say that removing 40-85% of an agent observation does not cost accuracy, and one says it improves it. A conservative reading for a default budget: the fold can afford to be aggressive, and a default that emits a small fraction of a page is supported by evidence rather than being a concession. (2) THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS THE TRAJECTORY, NOT THE PAGE -- 16.5% of context per observation still exhausts context in about six steps, so the per-step budget must be set by the expected interaction depth, not by what fits once. This is the single most actionable framing: choose the budget so that (expected steps x per-step tokens) sits well inside the context, and given the position-bias findings in item 30 that recency dominance sets in past roughly half the context fill, the target should be to stay under that half-fill point for the whole trajectory, not merely to fit. (3) SCREENSHOTS DO NOT EARN THEIR TOKENS: D2Snap's 'image input appears to add little to snapshot utility' with text-only grounding at 62% versus 73%, combined with the independent screenshot null result in item 28, is the most replicated finding in this area. (4) ORDER: nothing in this literature addresses where in the context high-value content should land, so the emission order must be decided from item 30's evidence rather than from here. What this literature does constrain is SHAPE -- preserve actionability-discriminating features, keep the structural frame, and drop redundancy -- which supports the complete-child-list-with-depth-truncation shape rather than a truncated linear prefix.
representation_cost: Raw DOM 10,000-100,000 tokens; 42% of raw snapshots over 128,000. Downsampled: D2Snap to a mean 16.5% context utilisation (roughly 21,000 tokens against a 128,000 window); PageDigest to 3,671 tokens from 6,437. So realistic post-downsampling costs span roughly 3,000-25,000 tokens per page depending on method and page, which is one to two orders of magnitude above a terse AXTree listing and one order below raw DOM. What is lost per token saved: attribute noise and redundant structure first (free), non-interactive wrappers second (cheap), then non-task-relevant content (costly for reading, free for acting), then structural distinctions (irrecoverable). The gradient matters -- the first 40-60% of reduction is nearly costless and the last 20% is where fidelity dies, and no paper reports the shape of that curve, which would be the most useful single figure the field could produce.
what_could_be_adopted: Five mechanisms and one methodological correction. (1) STRUCTURAL CONSOLIDATION IN THE D2SNAP SENSE -- collapse single-child chains, merge structurally identical repeated siblings into a representative plus a count, strip attributes not bearing on identity or interactivity -- because it is a pure deterministic function of the DOM, it is script-invariant, it needs no relevance model, and it is the direct analogue of the path compression the trie already performs. The framing of DOM downsampling as image compression for HTML is a good one and the sibling-collapse case is where the real gain lives. (2) THE ACTIONABILITY-DISCRIMINATING CRITERION as the retention rule: keep what you can act on and what distinguishes two actionable things from each other. This is the field's convergent answer, it is nearly identical to 'tag plus interactivity', and it is a structural criterion rather than a semantic one. (3) TRIMMING AS A SECURITY CONTROL (FocusAgent's argument), with the adaptive-adversary caveat attached and with MARKING preferred over silent dropping so that attempted injections leave evidence. (4) DOWNSAMPLE-FROM-STORED-CAPTURE rather than downsample-live, which makes the projection a re-runnable pure function over a lossless artifact and is what makes different budgets, A/B comparison and regression testing possible at all. No paper does this and it costs nothing. (5) ELISION MARKERS AND MONOTONICITY: mark every consolidation and drop with its class and count, and guarantee that a larger budget yields a superset. Together these turn downsampling from a lossy one-shot into a progressive-disclosure interface, which is what this project actually wants. METHODOLOGICAL CORRECTION: adopt an affordance-recall metric -- what fraction of a page's interactive elements and content survive downsampling -- rather than inferring fidelity from task success, because task success cannot see loss that the task did not need. The project already measures this (80.9% of affordances projected against 99.7% captured), which is a metric this literature does not have. Explicitly NOT to be adopted: LLM-generated pruning scripts (Prune4Web), which put a non-deterministic model inside the data path and destroy reproducibility; relevance- and task-conditioned trimming (FocusAgent, LineRetriever), which is a classifier over page regions; and visually-segmented region granularity, which imports geometry.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: SPLIT, AND THE SPLIT IS THE MAIN FINDING. Structural consolidation and actionability-based retention (D2Snap's core) are ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- they apply no semantic judgement, name no region, and use only tag, subtree shape and interactivity. Attribute pruning is ADOPTABLE AS-IS provided the retained-attribute set is a fixed mechanical vocabulary rather than a per-site tuned list. Relevance-, task- and query-conditioned pruning (FocusAgent, LineRetriever, PageDigest's digesting, Region4Web) is REJECTED: ranking page regions by task relevance is a classifier over regions in all but name. LLM-generated scoring scripts (Prune4Web) are REJECTED twice over -- as a learned relevance model and as a non-deterministic component in the data path. no_layout_in_the_fold: the text-in/text-out methods are ADOPTABLE AS-IS; any visually-segmented region granularity is ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY. o_delta: ADOPTABLE IN A BOUNDED FORM, WITH NAMED EXCEPTIONS. Structural consolidation is locally computable at O(affected subtree), but sibling-similarity collapsing amplifies a one-node change to its whole sibling group, and any GLOBAL TOKEN BUDGET is inherently non-local because adding content anywhere forces trimming elsewhere -- that is the fundamental exception and it means a budgeted projection is not O(delta) even when the underlying fold is. Relevance-based and LLM-generated pruning are O(page) per invocation with no incremental form and are REJECTED on this ground independently. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for the structural methods, which are real functions over real captured DOM. The FIGURES are NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY for the real web: four of the five methods are evaluated on five self-hosted simulated sites with no ads, consent overlays or third-party embeds, and the one live-web evaluation returned a confidence interval spanning zero. Quote the token reductions, do not quote the accuracy gains as established. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NO INTERACTION, and a GAP -- none of these papers mentions shadow DOM at all, so all of them implicitly assume a flat serialisation and none has been evaluated on a component-heavy page. That is an unaddressed correctness question, not a constraint violation. OVERALL VERDICT: take the structural half of this field as-is (consolidation, sibling collapsing, actionability retention, downsample-from-stored-capture, elision markers, monotone budgets); reject the relevance-conditioned and LLM-in-the-data-path half on structure_agnosticism and determinism; treat the accuracy numbers as suggestive and the token numbers as solid; and note that the field's own measured result -- that heavy compression costs nothing for acting -- says nothing about whether it costs something for reading, which is the question this project has to answer for itself.
governance_signal_handling: None; downsampling occurs after retrieval and none of these papers engages with robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF, Web Bot Auth or HTTP 402. One indirect relevance: because downsampling determines what content reaches a model, it is the natural enforcement point for any per-origin or per-region governance decision -- content from an origin whose signals forbid AI use could be excluded at this stage with an explicit marker rather than being silently included. No implementation does this and it would be straightforward given per-node provenance.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Downsampling is a data-minimisation mechanism whether or not it is designed as one: reducing an observation from 100,000 to 20,000 tokens reduces by the same proportion the third-party page content -- including personal data -- transmitted to any external model. That is a genuine privacy benefit and it argues for aggressive default budgets on grounds independent of cost. Two cautions. First, actionability-preserving retention specifically preserves FORM CONTROLS and their labels, which are the fields most likely to carry personal data, so an actionability-first downsampler concentrates rather than dilutes the PII in what survives -- the ratio improves while the sensitivity of the residue rises. Second, downsampled observations sent to a hosted model are a disclosure that leaves no trace in the stored artifact unless logged, so the retention question attaches to the transcript as much as to the capture. Erasure remains address-scoped and unaffected. [uncertain] on the specific lawful-basis analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject.
